newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe war veterans march on Mugabe in protest.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe war veterans march on Mugabe in protest.

text.p: Hundreds of angry Zimbabwean war veterans marched on President Robert Mugabe's official residence on Monday to protest against government handling of a war victims' compensation fund.
The protest took place as Mugabe, himself a former guerrilla leader in his country's independence war, announced a judicial commission to investigate charges of fraud and mismanagement of the fund.

About 800 independence war veterans marched through central Harare, stopping for about 30 minutes outside Mugabe's offices before proceeding to his residence, Zimbabwe House, one km (half a mile) away.
They protested as African leaders prepared to meet top U.S. businessmen in Zimbabwe to discuss business opportunities on the world's poorest continent.

U.S. President Bill Clinton is sending a delegation led by civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater to the four-day summit of African leaders and black Americans set to open in Harare on Tuesday.
The former guerrillas disrupted traffic as dozens of riot-control police armed with rifles, teargas and truncheons kept a low profile on the sidelines.

They carried placards, chanted slogans, shouted abuse at the government and sang revolutionary songs -- many the same ones they sang during a seven-year guerrilla war that led to Zimbabwe's independence in 1980.
They called on the government to pay immediately the compensation Mugabe suspended in March following allegations of abuse.
These included charges that some cabinet ministers ransacked the fund by claiming to have suffered up to 90 percent physical and mental disability during the 1970s war.

"Pay now or face trouble!" and "Come out and talk to us!" the ex-combatants shouted outside the heavily guarded presidential mansion, whose four-metre (13-foot) concrete wall is topped with an electric razor-wire.
Some presidential guards, armed with shotguns, truncheons and shields, patrolled around the demonstrators, some of whom vowed to picket outside until Mugabe addressed them.
Mugabe's aides said the president was locked in a meeting with colleagues from his ruling ZANU-PF party discussing the compensation issue.

On Sunday armed police had to rescue three cabinet ministers from a mob of veterans at a meeting in Harare to discuss compensation, which the ministers said would now resume on a case-by-case basis while investigations went on.

Zimbabwe state media said the veterans were in a "riotous mood" at several other meetings around the southern African state where Mugabe had sent cabinet ministers to explain the government's position. Some veterans threatened to beat up the ministers, accusing them of being thieves and liars.
On Monday, Mugabe said the judicial commission would investigate all payments between November 1980 and April 1987 and recommend how the government could recover money fraudulently drawn out.
